title: Overcoming the middle-income trap
lede_html: Martin Wolf's column on the World Bank's middle-income trap report, assigned for Session 6. Read it for two exam moves. Poor, middle-income and rich countries face different growth problems, which earns the first 2 marks of 2024 Q2c. And the gap that persists comes from using capital well or badly: TFP and the institutions under it, the story behind 2025 Q1 and Q2.

notes.quote: middle-income countries have exhibited higher growth rates than all others since the mid-1980s
notes.title: A faster growth rate is not the same as catching up
notes.body_html:
Patel and co-authors use this line to call the trap an outdated idea. A fast rate from a low base still leaves a huge level gap: further down, Wolf notes that middle-income incomes have stayed below 10% of the US every year since 1970.

The course reads convergence as conditional: the poorest countries of 1950 grew below the world average (S4). On 2025 Q3, file this fact under reasons to expect convergence and name the condition next to it.

notes.quote: 108 middle-income countries with incomes per capita of between US$1,136 and US$13,845
notes.title: Middle income is a twelvefold band
notes.body_html:
The World Bank counts 108 middle-income countries, with income per person between $1,136 and $13,845 a year. The top of the band is about twelve times the bottom.

13,845 ÷ 1,136 ≈ 12.2

That spread is why the WDR splits the band and prescribes a different strategy for each part.

notes.quote: the total population of the 34 middle-income economies that transitioned to high-income status since 1990 is less than 250 million, the population of Pakistan
notes.title: 34 countries escaped, but they hold under 250 million people
notes.body_html:
Count people, not countries. The 34 economies that reached high income since 1990 together hold fewer people than Pakistan. The WDR puts middle-income countries at about 6 billion people, so the escapees are about 4% of them.

0.25 billion ÷ 6 billion ≈ 4%

Use it as evidence that escape is rare, on the skeptical side of a convergence answer.

notes.title: Wolf says average; the WDR says median
notes.body_html: Wolf paraphrases the World Bank here. The report itself says the median income per capita of middle-income countries has never risen above 10% of the US level since 1970. If you cite the number, use the WDR wording, as the Session 6 prep page does.

notes.quote: the path that works for low-income countries will not work for more advanced ones
notes.title: Different stages, different growth problems
notes.body_html: This is the first move the 2024 Q2c key pays for: 2 marks for saying poor and middle-income countries face different growth problems from the US. A poor country still gains a lot from basic capital, because of diminishing returns. The key's own example: a water buffalo transforms a subsistence rice farm, while an expensive tractor barely moves a Canadian wheat farm.

notes.quote: the gap between GDP per worker in middle-income countries and the US is far greater than the gap in availability of physical and human capital
notes.title: The gap capital cannot explain is TFP
notes.body_html: Output per worker differs far more than capital and skills do. In the growth model, the part left over is total factor productivity: the technology, methods and organization that decide how well each machine and worker is used. Institutions sit underneath it. 2025 Q1 has the same shape: Mozambique's land is about as good as Germany's, yet it realizes about 18% of potential yield against about 83%.

notes.quote: the principal failure of middle-income countries lies not in accumulating too little capital, but in using it so poorly
notes.title: This line is about middle-income countries only
notes.body_html: Do not carry it into an answer about Mozambique or Africa. For low-income countries the WDR says investment comes first, and the 2025 key describes Mozambican farmers stuck with outdated tools on small, fragmented plots. The 2024 Q2c key gives 5 marks for capital deepening in poor countries. Too little capital is still their main problem.

notes.quote: openness to ideas from elsewhere (notably through direct investment and trade)
notes.title: Open trade carries ideas in
notes.body_html: Infusion needs skilled people who can absorb new methods, and openness through foreign direct investment and trade. Korea's export focus sped it up. The 2025 Q2 model answer lists a relatively open set of trade relations among Germany's key institutions. When you name open trade on the exam, add this channel: it brings in the machines, methods and know-how that raise TFP.

notes.quote: force incumbents to compete, encourage entrants and open the economy to those who were historically outsiders
notes.title: Creative destruction needs competition
notes.body_html: Schumpeter's idea, as Aghion and Howitt updated it: growth comes when entrants push out weaker incumbents and capital and workers move to better firms. Sheltered incumbents have little reason to adopt new technology. This is the lack of competition cause in the 2024 Q2b key. Session 8 puts a number on it for Canada: the six largest banks hold 94% of banking assets.

notes.quote: Part of the problem is the high cost of capital, itself the result of high levels of uncertainty
notes.title: Uncertainty makes capital expensive
notes.body_html: When outcomes are unpredictable, lenders charge more and fewer projects pay off. The 2025 Q3 credit rating is this point as a number: Mozambique's CCC+ against Germany's AAA means farmers and the government borrow at high cost, if at all. Wolf's fix is the institutions answer: rules that make returns predictable and secure lower the cost of capital, so more tractors, irrigation and storage get bought.

eyebrow: Reading 2 · Session 6 · World Bank main messages
sub: World Bank, August 2024 · the report behind Wolf's column
lede_html: The World Bank report Wolf summarizes. Read it for one framework: a country needs a different growth strategy at each income stage, from investment alone (1i) to investment plus infusion (2i) to all three with innovation (3i). The staircase sorts the past questions. Mozambique and Africa sit on the first step, and Session 8's AI op-ed asks Canada to act like the second.

notes.quote: since 1970, the median income per capita of middle-income countries has never risen above 10 percent of the US level
notes.title: The trap in one number
notes.body_html: For more than 50 years the typical middle-income country has stayed under a tenth of US income per person. Quote it as written: median, never above 10%. It shows that faster growth for a while has not closed the level gap, which is why the course calls convergence conditional.

notes.quote: a 2i strategy that emphasizes both investment and infusion, in which a country brings technologies from abroad and diffuses them domestically
notes.title: Infusion means adopting, not inventing
notes.body_html: Infusion is catch-up growth: bring in technology that already works abroad, then spread it across domestic firms. This answers Krugman in 2024 Q2c. The US sits at the frontier and must invent to grow; a poorer country can grow by copying. Session 8's op-ed asks Canada to treat AI the same way.

notes.quote: Low-income countries can focus solely on policies designed to increase investment
notes.title: Low income: investment comes first
notes.body_html: At low income the strategy is investment alone, because capital is scarce and each unit adds a lot of output. Mozambique and most of Africa sit on this step. An answer that prescribes innovation for them misses the 5 capital deepening marks in the 2024 Q2c key. Institutions still matter here: they decide whether anyone makes the investment.

notes.quote: At the upper-middle-income level, countries need to shift gears again to 3i
notes.title: The three i's in growth model terms
notes.body_html: Translate the WDR's words before you use them. Investment is capital deepening and skills. Infusion and innovation both raise TFP: one by adopting known ideas, the other by inventing new ones. Only the last step depends on invention, and that is where Krugman's US sits when he says growth is largely driven by innovation.

notes.quote: Median age
notes.title: Africa's base is wide: its workers are still to come
notes.body_html: Half of Africans are under 20, 39% are under 15 and only 4% are 65 or over. Over the next 15 years those children reach working age, so labour input rises and the dependency ratio can fall. That is the demographic dividend. It is a labour input gain: GDP per person rises once, as the working share rises.

This is the 2024 trilemma's third corner: cut immigration to cool housing, and the workforce ages and the dependency ratio rises.

notes.body_html: Sort the claim with the growth model before you judge it. More people is the labour input channel: it raises total GDP. Living standards need GDP per person to rise, which takes more output per worker or a larger share of people working. notes.show_quote: 2.5bn · Africa's projected population in 2050, up from 1.5bn
notes.title: 2.5 billion by 2050 means about 2.1% a year
notes.body_html:
Work out the rate the projection implies before you reason with it.

(2.5 ÷ 1.5)^(1/25) − 1 ≈ 0.021 ≈ 2.1% a year, 2025 to 2050

Each year's savings must first equip the new workers, so capital has to grow about 2.1% a year just to hold capital per worker flat. Slide 3's 1.57 billion is the more precise starting figure.

notes.title: 2.9% was the 1980s peak, not today's rate
notes.body_html: Modern medicine lifted Africa's population growth from 0.8% to 2.9% a year. At 2.9% a population doubles in about 24 years. The 2.5 billion projection implies about 2.1% from 2025, because fertility is expected to fall. The prep page's 2025 Q4 working assumes about 3% for Mozambique; call that an assumption when you use it.

notes.title: The hint: check both drivers of the growth model
notes.body_html: Fast growth touches both channels. Labour input rises later, but at about four children per woman the base keeps widening, so dependents stay high. Productivity suffers now: savings are spread over more new workers, so capital per worker barely rises. Close to 3% is the recent peak; the projection implies about 2.1%.

notes.quote: Rwanda (566 people per km²) and Burundi (533) are among Africa's densest countries and are low-income.
notes.title: Density is neither necessary nor sufficient
notes.body_html:
The densest countries here are poor and the sparsest are richer. Rwanda has about 140 times Botswana's density, yet it is low-income while Botswana is upper-middle-income. Sparse Canada and Australia are rich. One counterexample each way is enough to reject density as the most important reason.

notes.quote: institutions, not density, made the difference
notes.title: Reversal of fortune: institutions are the root
notes.body_html: Among former colonies, the places that were richest and densest in 1500 are relatively poor today. Density followed prosperity, and institutions decided which places stayed prosperous. This is the root cause argument of 2025 Q2: capital and people are proximate causes, and institutions decide whether anyone invests.

notes.quote: Rapid population growth spreads capital across more workers
notes.title: More people is labour input, not productivity
notes.body_html: This is the trap the practice question sets. More workers raise total GDP, but each one gets less capital unless investment keeps pace. Cheap, plentiful labour also gives firms little reason to buy machines. The dividend arrives only if fertility falls, so the working share rises.

notes.quote: Africa is urbanizing without industrializing
notes.title: Cities without factories skip the productivity jump
notes.body_html:
Structural transformation pays because workers move into jobs with more capital, specialization and scale. In Mozambique farms hold 70% of jobs but make 25% of GDP, so a worker who leaves produces about seven times as much on average. Africa's cities are fed by resource exports, so the jobs that deliver that jump are scarce. 2025 Q4 wants the term structural transformation by name.

title: Session 8 slides: Spiky Canada
lede_html: Session 8's deck on Canada's economy and AI. The prep page's 2024 Q2b answer and its Canada section take their numbers from slides 3 and 30, and the key's list of causes (resources, competition, small market) maps onto the group slides. Most of these figures are newer than both past papers: cite them as current evidence and keep their years.

notes.quote: Canada should approach AI more like a middle-income country, absorbing and spreading the world's best technology, than like a frontier economy trying to invent it.
notes.title: Canada on the WDR staircase
notes.body_html: The Session 8 op-ed borrows the WDR's 3i ladder. Its bet is that Canada's AI gains come from infusion: adopt the best technology and spread it across firms. This is the answer to Krugman turned on a rich country: you can grow by using what already exists.

notes.quote: invested per worker for every U.S. dollar, 2024
notes.show_quote: 54¢ invested per worker for every U.S. dollar, 2024. Down from 87¢ in 2014.
notes.title: 54 cents per US dollar of investment per worker
notes.body_html: For every dollar a US business invests per worker, a Canadian business invests 54¢, down from 87¢ in 2014. The ratio fell about 38% in a decade. Less capital per worker means slower productivity growth. The prep page's 2024 Q2b answer names this as its first cause.

notes.quote: capital per worker since 2015
notes.show_quote: −9% capital per worker since 2015. Machinery and equipment per worker are down about 20%.
notes.title: −9% means capital deepening ran in reverse
notes.body_html: This number is not a ratio to the US. Each Canadian worker has about 9% less capital than in 2015, and about 20% less machinery and equipment. Capital per worker fell while the population grew fast, so productivity lost its main lever. Do not mix it up with the 54¢ next to it.

notes.show_quote: 73% business productivity vs the U.S., 2019. Down from 83% in 2002.
notes.title: 73% is a 2019 figure
notes.body_html: Business productivity slid from 83% of the US level in 2002 to 73% in 2019. The gap widened from 17 to 27 points over two decades, which is the 2-mark point in 2024 Q2b. The latest year here is 2019, so write by 2019, not today.

notes.quote: points of the Canada–U.S. productivity gap due to firm-size mix
notes.show_quote: 6 of 27 points of the Canada–U.S. productivity gap due to firm-size mix. 2019. Canada was at 73% of U.S. productivity.
notes.title: Small firms explain 6 of the 27 points
notes.body_html: In 2019 Canada was at 73% of US productivity, a 27-point gap. Canada's heavier mix of small firms explains 6 of those points. Small Canadian firms reach only 70% of their US peers, large ones 87%. This is the key's small market cause: a small home market limits returns to scale.

notes.quote: of merchandise exports are natural-resource products
notes.show_quote: 53% of merchandise exports are natural-resource products. 2024, including energy. 75% of them go to the U.S.
notes.title: A resource economy: high productivity, slow growth
notes.body_html: Natural-resource products make up 53% of merchandise exports, and 75% of them go to the US. The 2024 Q2b key lists over-exposure to resources as a cause: these industries are highly productive, but their productivity grows slowly. Their prices also swing hard: Canada's commodity price index fell 42% from 2014 to 2016.

notes.quote: of banking assets are held by the six largest banks
notes.show_quote: 94% of banking assets are held by the six largest banks
notes.title: Lack of competition, in numbers
notes.body_html: Six banks hold 94% of banking assets and three carriers have 86% of mobile subscribers. Canada ranks 26th of 38 on the OECD's product-market regulation index, down from 10th in 1998: its rules now restrict competition more than most rich countries'. Firms sheltered from rivals feel little pressure to invest or adopt. This is the lack of competition cause in the 2024 Q2b key.

notes.show_quote: 3.2% population growth in 2023. The fastest since 1957. 98% came from international migration.
notes.title: 3.2%: two framings, quote one
notes.body_html: This slide says 3.2% in 2023, the fastest since 1957, with 98% from international migration. Session 2 frames the same 3.2% as 2023 to 24, the fastest in the G7. The prep page says to quote one framing, and its answer uses this one. Either way it is the yes in 2024 Q2b: more people, more workers, more total GDP.

notes.show_quote: −1.3% · −1.4% change in real GDP per person, 2023 · 2024. As first published. Total real GDP grew in both years.
notes.title: The but: GDP per person fell in both years
notes.body_html: Total real GDP grew, but real GDP per person fell 1.3% in 2023 and 1.4% in 2024, as first published. This is the 3-mark but in 2024 Q2b: growth came almost entirely from labour force growth, and living standards follow GDP per person. Put the two numbers side by side, as the prep page's answer does.

notes.quote: population growth, July 2025 to July 2026
notes.show_quote: 0.5% population growth, July 2025 to July 2026. The lowest July-to-July rate in over a century.
notes.title: Now the labour input engine has stalled
notes.body_html: Population growth fell to 0.5%, the lowest July-to-July rate in over a century. With labour input slowing, growth in GDP per person has to come from productivity. This is the trilemma's housing plus productivity corner in practice: less immigration eases housing demand, but the workforce ages faster. Both past papers predate these figures.

notes.quote: residential investment as a share of GDP: Canada vs U.S.
notes.show_quote: 8.3% vs 4.2% residential investment as a share of GDP: Canada vs U.S. Average, 2018–2023.
notes.title: Canada pours capital into housing
notes.body_html: Canada puts 8.3% of GDP into residential investment, about twice the US's 4.2% (2018 to 2023 average). The 2024 Q1a key calls residential construction a chronically low and declining productivity sector. Every dollar and builder used on housing is one not used to raise productivity, which is the hinge of the trilemma.
